claims.claim: Jupiter is the biggest planet in the solar system.
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/index.html; jupiterfact.html
claims.note: Fact sheet: Jupiter has the largest mass (1898e24 kg) and diameter of the eight planets; volumetric mean radius 69,911 km vs Saturn 58,232 km. A4: the first sentence alone is true and leaves no false impression.

claims.claim: Two and a half times the mass of every other planet combined.
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/index.html and the eight per-planet fact sheets
claims.note: Per-planet sheets: Jupiter 1898.13e24 kg; others 0.33010+4.8673+5.9722+0.64169+568.32+86.811+102.409 = 769.3e24 kg; ratio 2.47 (index-table values give 2.47 too). 'Two and a half' is a fair rounding.

claims.claim: JUPITER / 2.5× the other planets / combined, by mass
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/index.html and per-planet fact sheets
claims.note: Same arithmetic as claim 2: ratio 2.47, shown as 2.5×, and the label says by mass.

claims.claim: Jupiter at radius 96 with the other seven planets beneath at the same scale: Saturn 0.833, Uranus 0.363, Neptune 0.352, Earth 0.091, Venus 0.087, Mars 0.0485, Mercury 0.035 of Jupiter's radius
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/<planet>fact.html for all eight planets (volumetric mean radius)
claims.note: Volumetric mean radii / 69,911 km: Saturn 58,232 → 0.8329; Uranus 25,362 → 0.3628; Neptune 24,622 → 0.3522; Earth 6,371.0 → 0.0911; Venus 6,051.8 → 0.0866; Mars 3,389.5 → 0.0485; Mercury 2,439.7 → 0.0349. All drawn values match to the stated precision.

claims.claim: But hold Jupiter up next to the Sun, and it looks tiny.
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/sunfact.html; jupiterfact.html
claims.note: Sun volumetric mean radius 695,700 km vs Jupiter 69,911 km: Jupiter is 1/9.95 of the Sun's width. 'Looks tiny' is a fair description of a 10:1 disc.

claims.claim: Jupiter drawn at radius 52 beside the Sun at radius 520
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/sunfact.html; jupiterfact.html
claims.note: Drawn ratio 10.0 vs true 9.95 (695,700/69,911). To scale within 0.5%.

claims.claim: It would take nearly a thousand Jupiters to fill the Sun.
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/sunfact.html (Volume 1,412,000 x10^12 km^3); jupiterfact.html (Volume 143,128 x10^10 km^3 = 1,431.28 x10^12)
claims.note: Volume ratio 986.5 (radius cubed gives 985), so 'nearly a thousand' is right and does not overstate. It is a volume comparison (solid spheres would pack worse), which the on-screen sub 'by volume' states while the line is on screen.

claims.claim: ≈ 1,000 JUPITERS / to fill it, by volume / dots not to scale, over 1,000 small dots across the Sun's disc
claims.source_checked: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/sunfact.html; jupiterfact.html
claims.note: 986.5 shown as ≈ 1,000; 'by volume' qualifies the count; the dots are smaller than Jupiter and are labelled not to scale (A6). Mass ratio 1,988,400/1,898.13 = 1,048 is a different number and is not claimed.

claims.claim: Our Sun is not an average star. It is an unusually big one.
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021, A&A 650, A201, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (arXiv:2104.14972 LaTeX source: Table 3 'Summary of the 10 pc sample' (tab:numbers), Sect. 4 text on the 41 untyped objects and on evolved stars); Boyajian et al. 2012, ApJ 757, 112, doi:10.1088/0004-637X/757/2/112 (arXiv:1208.2431 LaTeX source, fund_params_combined.tex = Table 6 'Fundamental Parameters', 6th table input in ms.tex); Giammichele, Bergeron & Dufour 2012, ApJS 199, 29, doi:10.1088/0067-0049/199/2/29 (arXiv:1202.5581 LaTeX source, tab2.tex = Table 2, all 165 rows parsed); Thévenin et al. 2005, A&A 436, 253, doi:10.1051/0004-6361:20042075 (Crossref metadata; arXiv:astro-ph/0501420 LaTeX source, results table)
claims.note: Table 3 (Sun excluded): A 4, F 8, G 18, K 38, M 249, D 20, N/A 41. Only G-or-hotter stars (30, plus the Sun) can match it; K and M dwarfs (Boyajian Table 6: largest K 0.831 R_sun, M dwarfs <= 0.5773 R_sun) and white dwarfs (Giammichele Table 2: <= 0.022 R_sun by Stefan-Boltzmann) are smaller. 'Unusually big' = bigger than ~91% of the census; supported by the narrower reading of the numbers.

claims.claim: It is bigger and brighter than over ninety percent of the stars in our part of the galaxy
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021, A&A 650, A201, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (arXiv:2104.14972 LaTeX source: Table 3 'Summary of the 10 pc sample' (tab:numbers), Sect. 4 text on the 41 untyped objects and on evolved stars); Boyajian et al. 2012, ApJ 757, 112, doi:10.1088/0004-637X/757/2/112 (arXiv:1208.2431 LaTeX source, fund_params_combined.tex = Table 6 'Fundamental Parameters', 6th table input in ms.tex); Giammichele, Bergeron & Dufour 2012, ApJS 199, 29, doi:10.1088/0067-0049/199/2/29 (arXiv:1202.5581 LaTeX source, tab2.tex = Table 2, all 165 rows parsed); Thévenin et al. 2005, A&A 436, 253, doi:10.1051/0004-6361:20042075 (Crossref metadata; arXiv:astro-ph/0501420 LaTeX source, results table)
claims.note: Worst case (every A/F/G star counted as bigger and brighter): Sun exceeds K+M+D = 307 of 337 typed stars; Reylé Sect. 4 says there is no giant within 10 pc and only four subgiants (beta Hyi, mu Her Aa, delta Pav, delta Eri), delta Eri being the only K one; Thévenin 2005 gives delta Eri (K0 IV) R = 2.33 R_sun, L = 3.19 L_sun, so remove it: 306/337 = 90.8%. Brighter: Boyajian K/M L <= 0.53 L_sun; Giammichele brightest WD log L = -1.12 (Sirius B within 10 pc -1.53). Reylé says the 41 untyped are all close-binary secondaries: 36 possible M, 4 possible L, 1 possible WD, so including them raises the share (~91.7%). 'Over ninety percent' holds, thin margin. Scope: the census is the 10 pc sample, which the script calls 'our part of the galaxy' and the screen 'nearby'.

claims.claim: THE SUN / bigger than 9 in 10 nearby stars
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021, A&A 650, A201, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (arXiv:2104.14972 LaTeX source: Table 3 'Summary of the 10 pc sample' (tab:numbers), Sect. 4 text on the 41 untyped objects and on evolved stars); Boyajian et al. 2012, ApJ 757, 112, doi:10.1088/0004-637X/757/2/112 (arXiv:1208.2431 LaTeX source, fund_params_combined.tex = Table 6 'Fundamental Parameters', 6th table input in ms.tex); Giammichele, Bergeron & Dufour 2012, ApJS 199, 29, doi:10.1088/0067-0049/199/2/29 (arXiv:1202.5581 LaTeX source, tab2.tex = Table 2, all 165 rows parsed); Thévenin et al. 2005, A&A 436, 253, doi:10.1051/0004-6361:20042075 (Crossref metadata; arXiv:astro-ph/0501420 LaTeX source, results table)
claims.note: Same numbers as claim 10: 306/337 = 90.8% worst case, higher with untyped companions included. 'Nearby' matches the 10 pc census.

claims.claim: because most of them are red dwarfs: small, dim, and everywhere.
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021, A&A 650, A201, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (arXiv:2104.14972 LaTeX source: Table 3 'Summary of the 10 pc sample' (tab:numbers), Sect. 4 text on the 41 untyped objects and on evolved stars); Boyajian et al. 2012, ApJ 757, 112, doi:10.1088/0004-637X/757/2/112 (arXiv:1208.2431 LaTeX source, fund_params_combined.tex = Table 6 'Fundamental Parameters', 6th table input in ms.tex)
claims.note: Table 3: M 249 of 337 typed stars = 74% (285/374 = 76% with the 36 possible-M untyped). Paper's own figure 58.9 ± 5.8% of 423 typed objects including brown dwarfs, 61.3 ± 5.9% with untyped: a majority on every reading. Small and dim: Boyajian Table 6 M dwarfs 0.141-0.5773 R_sun, 0.00155-0.0697 L_sun. 'Because' is fair: red dwarfs are the bulk of the stars the Sun out-sizes (with K dwarfs and white dwarfs making up the rest).

claims.claim: 10×10 grid of 100 dots: 8 large bright yellow (G or hotter), 10 orange (K), 5 tiny white (white dwarfs), 77 red (M or untyped); label 'dots: star type, not size'
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021, A&A 650, A201, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (arXiv:2104.14972 LaTeX source: Table 3 'Summary of the 10 pc sample' (tab:numbers), Sect. 4 text on the 41 untyped objects and on evolved stars)
claims.note: Per 100 of 379 (337 typed + 41 untyped + Sun): G-or-hotter 31 → 8.2; K 38 → 10.0; D 20 → 5.3; M 249 + untyped 41 = 290 → 76.5. Rounded 8/10/5/77 sums to 100. Reylé assigns the 41 untyped as 36 possible M, 4 possible L, 1 possible WD; moving those 5 changes at most one dot, within rounding. The label discloses that dot size is not star size (A6).

claims.claim: So look at the nearest star to our own. Proxima Centauri ... The closest star to the Sun
claims.source_checked: Anglada-Escudé et al. 2016, Nature 536, 437, doi:10.1038/nature19106 (arXiv:1609.03449 LaTeX source, opening paragraph); NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP, pscomppars where hostname like 'Proxima%' (sy_dist, sy_vmag, st_spectype, st_rad)
claims.note: Source text: 'At a distance of 1.295 parsecs, the red-dwarf Proxima Centauri ... is the Sun's closest stellar neighbour'. Wording 'nearest star to our own' / 'closest star to the Sun' matches.

claims.claim: Proxima Centauri, just over four light years away.
claims.source_checked: NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP, pscomppars where hostname like 'Proxima%' (sy_dist, sy_vmag, st_spectype, st_rad)
claims.note: sy_dist = 1.30119 (+0.00034/-0.00035) pc = 4.244 ly (1 pc = 3.2616 ly); Anglada-Escudé 2016 gives 1.295 pc = 4.22 ly. 'Just over four' is accurate.

claims.claim: PROXIMA CENTAURI / ≈ 1/7 the Sun's radius (drawn at radius 13.7 against the Sun's 96)
claims.source_checked: Kervella et al. 2017, A&A 598, L7, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/201629930 (arXiv:1611.03495 LaTeX source, macros RProx/RProxMann and Sect. on radius); Boyajian et al. 2012, ApJ 757, 112, doi:10.1088/0004-637X/757/2/112 (arXiv:1208.2431 LaTeX source, fund_params_combined.tex = Table 6 'Fundamental Parameters', 6th table input in ms.tex) row GJ 551; NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP, pscomppars where hostname like 'Proxima%' (sy_dist, sy_vmag, st_spectype, st_rad)
claims.note: Interferometric radius 0.141 ± 0.007 R_sun (Demory 2009, quoted by Kervella and in Boyajian Table 6 row GJ 551); Kervella's model-based 0.1542 ± 0.0045 is +1.6 sigma larger; Archive 0.141 ± 0.021. 1/7 = 0.143 and 13.7/96 = 0.143 sit inside the measured and Archive ranges; '≈' covers the model value's spread.

claims.claim: you have almost certainly never seen it.
claims.source_checked: NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP, pscomppars where hostname like 'Proxima%' (sy_dist, sy_vmag, st_spectype, st_rad); Howard et al. 2018, ApJL 860, L30, doi:10.3847/2041-8213/aacaf3 (arXiv:1804.02001 LaTeX source, abstract and Sect. 3)
claims.note: Archive sy_vmag = 11.01, far below naked-eye limits. Howard: 'no M-dwarfs are usually visible to the naked-eye'; its one naked-eye-brightness superflare (2016 March 18, ~68x) reached g' = 6.8, 'at the limit of visibility to trained observers at very dark sites'. 'Almost certainly' is properly hedged.

claims.claim: It is almost always too faint for your eyes.
claims.source_checked: NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP, pscomppars where hostname like 'Proxima%' (sy_dist, sy_vmag, st_spectype, st_rad); Howard et al. 2018 (arXiv:1804.02001, as above)
claims.note: Quiescent V = 11.01 (g' = 11.4 per Howard); only the rare superflare briefly brought it to the naked-eye limit, so 'almost always' matches the source.

claims.claim: That is what most of the stars around us look like. (the 8 bright dots fade out)
claims.source_checked: NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP, pscomppars where hostname like 'Proxima%' (sy_dist, sy_vmag, st_spectype, st_rad) (st_spectype M5.5 V); Reylé et al. 2021, A&A 650, A201, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (arXiv:2104.14972 LaTeX source: Table 3 'Summary of the 10 pc sample' (tab:numbers), Sect. 4 text on the 41 untyped objects and on evolved stars)
claims.note: Proxima is M5.5 V; M dwarfs are 249 of 337 typed stars within 10 pc (74%), so most nearby stars are faint red dwarfs like it. The fade leaves K, M and white-dwarf dots: all smaller and dimmer than the Sun (claim 10), consistent with the line.

claims.claim: The star we call ordinary is one of the rare big ones.
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021, A&A 650, A201, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (arXiv:2104.14972 LaTeX source: Table 3 'Summary of the 10 pc sample' (tab:numbers), Sect. 4 text on the 41 untyped objects and on evolved stars); Boyajian et al. 2012, ApJ 757, 112, doi:10.1088/0004-637X/757/2/112 (arXiv:1208.2431 LaTeX source, fund_params_combined.tex = Table 6 'Fundamental Parameters', 6th table input in ms.tex); Giammichele, Bergeron & Dufour 2012, ApJS 199, 29, doi:10.1088/0067-0049/199/2/29 (arXiv:1202.5581 LaTeX source, tab2.tex = Table 2, all 165 rows parsed)
claims.note: G-or-hotter stars including the Sun: 4 + 8 + 18 + 1 = 31 of 379 (8%) - rare. The Sun is in that group and is bigger than >= 90.8% of the census (claim 10), so 'one of the rare big ones' is supported.

claims.claim: THE SUN / one of the few (Sun shrinks into the grid as one of the 8 bright dots)
claims.source_checked: Reylé et al. 2021, A&A 650, A201, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (arXiv:2104.14972 LaTeX source: Table 3 'Summary of the 10 pc sample' (tab:numbers), Sect. 4 text on the 41 untyped objects and on evolved stars)
claims.note: 31/379 = 8.2% → 8 dots of 100, the Sun among them (A 4 + F 8 + G 18 + Sun). Matches.
